newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai authorities to discuss zero-tariff soymeal.
newsitem.headline: Thai authorities to discuss zero-tariff soymeal.

text.p: Thai authorities will soon discuss the possible elimination of the current 10 percent soymeal import tariff, a senior Commerce Ministry official said on Friday.

Siriphol Yodmaungcharoen, deputy director-general of the Internal Trade Department, told reporters the ministry will submit the proposal by the feed industry to the government-run Food Policy Committee for consideration.

"We have held meetings with concerned sectors -- the animal feed industry, the end users, the oil crushers and agricultural officials -- to sound out their opinions. We'll try our best to be fair to all sides," he said.
The animal feed industry and oil crushers have often clashed over soymeal and soybean import tariffs.
Since the price of vegetable oil is controlled, the government allows oil crushers to import soybeans tariff-free. After crushing, the industry also sells by-product soymeal on the market.

Oil crushers were often criticised by the animal feed industry as over-privileged and for reaping lucrative profits by selling the oil while at the same time commanding high prices for soymeal which they produce at low cost.
Animal feed producers, citing soaring prices of soymeal, say the soymeal import tariff must be removed or high production costs will drive up prices of meat.
Prasit Damrongchietanon, president of the Thai Feed Mill Association, told Reuters the price of soymeal has increased an average of $70 per tonne from the last quarter of 1996.
"The soymeal prices rose sharply and affected the cost of production and consequently the price stability of foods," he said.
Prasit projected soymeal demand this year to reach 1.8 million tonnes, about 1.0 million of which will be imported.

However, Settasarn Settakarun, a consultant to the Thai Cottonseed, Ricebran and Vegetable Oil Crushers Association, said any cut in the soymeal import tariff would have little positive effect on production costs but would harm local soybean farmers.
He said the removal of the tariffs will reduce the cost of raising chicken by only about 24 satang (1 U.S. cent) per kg of chicken meat.

"But it will push local soybean prices down by 85 satang a kg. Removing soymeal tariffs is not the answer...The cost of running the livestock industry does not depend on the soybean alone. If one wants to cut costs, there are other things one can do," he said. ($1 = 26 baht)
